title: Vowel harmony and plurals
intro: Most Turkish suffixes change their vowel to match the word they join. This is vowel harmony (*ünlü uyumu*), and it is the key to everything that follows. This unit sorts the eight vowels into groups, uses them to build the plural with *-lar* or *-ler*, and adds the words for this and that, and for a or one.

blocks.text: Turkish has eight vowels. Two questions sort them. Is the vowel made at the **front** or the **back** of the mouth? And are the lips **rounded** or not? Say *e* then *a*: your tongue moves back. Say *i* then *ü*: your lips round.
For now you only need the first question, front or back: it decides two-way harmony below. Rounding joins in with four-way harmony in [unit 3](a1-u03).
What matters is always the **last** vowel of the word, whatever comes before it:
Learn the two groups as two short chants: front *e, i, ö, ü*; back *a, ı, o, u*. The dotless *ı* is a back vowel; the dotted *i* is a front one.

Many suffixes come in two forms, one with *e* and one with *a*. Which one you use depends on the last vowel of the word: after a front vowel the suffix takes *e*, after a back vowel it takes *a*. This is two-way harmony.

blocks.label: Two-way harmony
lines: last vowel e, i, ö, ü  →  suffix with e
last vowel a, ı, o, u  →  suffix with a

blocks.text: The plural is the first suffix of this kind: *-ler* after front vowels, *-lar* after back vowels. Only the last vowel counts, however long the word is: *bilgisayar* has i, i, a, a, and the last one is a, so its plural is *bilgisayarlar*.

Harmony is not a spelling rule added on top of the language: it makes words easier to say, because the tongue stays in the same part of the mouth. Say *evlar* and *evler* aloud, and *evler* will feel smoother.
Look at the **last** vowel, not the first: *pencere* → *pencereler*, but *araba* → *arabalar*. And never use *ı, i, u* or *ü* in a two-way suffix: there is no *-lır* or *-lür*.
Add *-lar* or *-ler* to a noun to make it plural. The ending never changes the word in front of it, and it takes the stress: *kaLEM*, *kalemLER*.

Turkish uses the plural less than English does. After a number or a word of quantity, the noun stays singular: *iki kalem* (two pens), *çok kitap* (many books). You'll practise numbers in [unit 11](a1-u11).
Some fixed phrases use the plural where English doesn't. You met three in [unit 1](a1-u01): *iyi akşamlar*, *iyi geceler* and *teşekkürler* are literally good evenings, good nights and thanks.
Don't add the plural after a number: *iki kalem*, never *iki kalemler*.

sections.title: This and that: bu, şu, o

blocks.text: Turkish has three words where English has two. *Bu* is this, for something near the speaker. *Şu* is that, for something a little farther away, often something you point at. *O* is that over there, farther away or out of sight.

Each word works in two ways. Before a noun it is an adjective and never changes: *bu kitap* (this book), *bu kitaplar* (these books). On its own it is a pronoun, and then it has a plural with an extra *n*: *bunlar*, *şunlar*, *onlar*.

Notice Emre's answer. After a plural pronoun like *şunlar*, the noun that names the things can stay singular: *Şunlar defter* (those are notebooks), or just *Defter*. You will also hear *Şunlar defterler*; both are correct.
Before a noun, always use *bu*, *şu* or *o*, even in the plural: *bu kitaplar*, never *bunlar kitaplar*. *O* is also the word for he, she and it, which you'll meet in [unit 3](gp-personal-pronouns).
*Bir* is the number one, and it also works like **a** or **an**. Turkish has no word for **the**: *kalem* on its own can mean a pen or the pen, and the situation tells you which.

When there is an adjective, *bir* goes **after** it, right before the noun: *yeni bir kitap* (a new book), *büyük bir masa* (a big table). Adjectives come before the noun and never change for the plural: *yeni kitaplar* (new books).

lines: bir + noun               bir çanta           a bag
adjective + bir + noun   kırmızı bir çanta   a red bag

blocks.text: Without *bir*, *Bu kitap* can be read two ways: this book, or this is a book. *Bir* makes the sentence clear: *Bu bir kitap*. And *bir* is only for one thing, so it never goes with a plural.
*Bir* before the adjective sounds like you are counting: *bir yeni kitap* is one new book. For a new book, say *yeni bir kitap*.
Like French “un”, *bir* is both the number and the article. Unlike French, Turkish has no gender and no word for the definite article.

Many Turkish words were borrowed from Arabic, Persian, French and Italian, and some of them have vowels from both groups: *kitap* (i, a), *otobüs* (o, ü), *telefon* (e, o). These are not really exceptions: like every word, they follow their **last** vowel.

The real exceptions are a small group of loanwords, mostly from Arabic and French, that take front suffixes even though their last vowel is back. They do so for historical reasons, and nothing in the spelling predicts it, so learn them as you meet them. A good dictionary shows the plural.
*Saat* also means hour and o'clock: *Saat kaç?* (What time is it?) comes in [unit 11](gp-telling-time).

summary: Front vowels: *e, i, ö, ü*. Back vowels: *a, ı, o, u*.
The last vowel of a word decides the suffix: *e* after a front vowel, *a* after a back vowel.
The plural is *-lar* or *-ler*: *kitaplar*, *kalemler*. It is not used after numbers: *iki kalem*.
*Bu*, *şu* and *o* mean this, that, and that over there; as pronouns their plurals are *bunlar*, *şunlar*, *onlar*.
Before a noun the demonstrative never changes: *bu kitaplar*.
*Bir* means one and a; with an adjective it comes after it: *yeni bir kitap*.
A few loanwords take front suffixes: *saatler*, *harfler*, *roller*.
